messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Distribution of standard deviations
parts:
> On Apr 26, 2017, at 12:18 PM, Gregory <gregor...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello everyone
>
> My question may be more theoretical than technical, but I'm building a model to approximate a task where users aim to correctly place a series of objects on a continuous scale. Some objects are more difficult to place correctly than others however, and therefore the variances for some placements are higher than are others. I'd like to model these parameters hierarchically, because some objects are not rated by many users or only by a single user (the latter of which are therefore not identified). My first thought was to model these with a gamma distribution, but is it more reasonable to use a normal or something else?

This is a kind of multiple rater problem making it a lot like IRT.
You want a component of variance to come from the user and one component
of the variance to come from the item.

You may also want to model a bias (mean) from the user and from
the item (let's say you're placing colors on a spectrum and some
users may tend more toward the red side than others; or let's say
you have some color that somehow looks more red than it is [context
maybe] and causes users to judge it as more red than it really is.

> If I can put this more concretely by analogy: among professional archers, each archer has a variance on the distance of his or her shots from the bulleye. Assuming unbiasedness in shots, low variance means that an archer typically hits close to the target; high variance, the archer typically hits far from the target. Imagine we know the variances for all archers. Would one want to model these as gamma distributed? Normally distributed? Otherwise?

We'd want to plot what all those variances looked like to get an
idea of which distribution to use. It's not a theoretical question.
In practice, it may not matter much, especially if you have more than
a few dozen observations.

You also want to look at how the abilities of the users and the
difficulties of the items interact. Are they additive or are there
interactions?

- Bob
